title: Cave, Cape and World Stone: Kin Across Five Centuries
standfirst: On Okinawa's east coast, a monk's limestone cave, a coral-reef bay and a stone carved with an emigrant's vow explain a town shaped by leaving and returning: centuries as a Ryukyuan district, the age of emigration to Hawaii and the Philippines, a wartime prisoner camp, and the Marine Corps base that today covers much of Kin.

sections.heading: A cape, a bay and a cave

paragraphs.text: Kin sits on the narrow waist of central Okinawa, where a stubby peninsula and its fringing reef enclose Kin Bay on the island's Pacific side. The Japanese Navy's 1908 pilot guide to these waters charts the bay as a broad, open anchorage exposed to the east and south, its mouth spanned by reef ground reaching about two miles between Kin Cape and the islets of Tsuken and Kudaka; a county gazetteer published in Naha eleven years later borrows the same survey when it describes the cape's reef running two-thirds of a mile out to sea. That 1919 book, written for Kunigami County by the schoolteacher and local historian Shimabukuro Genichiro, also names the peaks behind the town, Kin-dake and Igei-dake, and lists the harbors strung along the coast that Kin village then administered: Ginoza, Kanna and Fukuhana ports to the north, as well as Kin's own anchorage at Tomikura.

The 1908 pilot guide is worth pausing on for another reason: it romanizes the bay as "Chimu Wan" and the cape as "Chimu Saki", the old reading of the place name 金武 used by surveyors and, later, by the wartime US forces who built an airstrip on the peninsula and knew it as Chimu Airfield. The same 1919 gazetteer records that in the 1670s, in the Ryukyu Kingdom's own administrative reshuffling, land was cut from Nago and from Kin to found the new district of Kushi — evidence that Kin already existed as an established magiri, or district, more than three and a half centuries ago, its bounds at that time reaching inland to take in the hamlets that would only in the twentieth century become the separate village of Ginoza.

Local tradition places another arrival on this coast two centuries earlier still. A wandering monk named Nisshu, born in Kii province around 1503, is said to have set out on a votive sea voyage in search of Kannon's paradise across the southern seas, been driven off course, and washed up at Kin's small port of Fukka in 1522. Finding a deep limestone cave open to the shore, he is said to have taken it for a dwelling of the bodhisattva Kannon, carved three images for it with his own hands, and founded the temple that still stands over the cave mouth as Kimpuzan Kin Kannon-ji. Nisshu went on, by the same tradition, to restore Naminoue Shrine and Gokoku-ji in Naha before ending his life in Satsuma; the 1919 county gazetteer already lists his grave, the temple and the port of Fukka among Kin village's "notable places and historic remains", confirming that the story was well established locally within four centuries of the event it describes.

sections.heading: The village that sent its sons to Hawaii

paragraphs.text: Kin's modern fame rests on a single, closely dated episode. Toyama Kyuzo, a Kin-born teacher and prefectural assemblyman, spent the 1890s lobbying Okinawa's government to let islanders emigrate for work, against officials who feared the loss of labor, remittances, and face. Failing to move them, he organized the passage privately: a party left Naha and sailed from Yokohama on the steamer China, and on 8 January 1900 twenty-six contract laborers walked onto the Honolulu docks to begin work on Oahu's sugar plantations. Okinawa's prefectural archives record that ten of the twenty-six were young men from Kin itself. From his own village, Toyama had opened a migration that the archives put at about 3,225 people sent abroad from Kin by the time the war cut off overseas emigration in 1941.

Toyama did not stop at Hawaii. A letter he wrote in September 1907 to a former comrade from Okinawa's freedom-and-rights movement, Taira Shinsuke, by then settled in North America, claims credit for having already sent about five thousand Okinawans abroad — some four thousand to Hawaii and the rest to Mexico, Peru, New Caledonia, the Philippines and Canada — and describes the whole prefecture as "day and night absorbed in plans for going overseas". He had already started an emigrants' newspaper to shield migrants from predatory brokers, and was preparing to found a protective association to do the same. A guidebook to Ryukyu published in 1926, sixteen years after Toyama's death, still measured his legacy in the household economics of his own village: villagers of Kin, it reports, had by mutual agreement capped their evening drinking to five go of awamori a month — and were keeping to it — the book's own example of a new frugality then spreading across the prefecture.

The same 1926 book locates Toyama's memorial in the landscape rather than in a museum case: his defiant call to leave — "Let us go: our home is the five continents" — was cut into a stone that still stands on a low hill in Kin, a stone that villagers had already taken to calling simply the "World Stone". A matching marble stone from Kin, carrying the same verse, was unveiled at the Hawaii Okinawa Center in Honolulu in January 2000 to mark the centenary of the crossing.

Hawaii is the destination Kin is remembered for, but two directories of overseas Okinawans compiled in the late 1930s show a second, less celebrated stream running to the Philippines. Abaca — Manila hemp, the fiber crop that supplied the world's rope — drew thousands of Okinawan laborers to plantations around Davao on Mindanao from the 1900s, many of them recruited through the Japanese firm Ota Kogyo. A 1937 directory of Japanese abroad and a 1938 gazetteer of prominent Okinawans between them name a run of Kin men who made that crossing: Igei Man'ei, born in Kin in 1892, who landed at Davao in 1912 and went to work for Ota Kogyo; Tsukayama Chosho, from Kin's Kanna hamlet, who reached the Davao anchorage of Talomo in August 1918 to grow abaca and later headed a branch of the local Japanese association; and Shimabukuro Chujiro, from Kin's Kochiya hamlet, who landed at Davao in 1919, worked the Royan plantation for two years, then joined Ota Kogyo's Santiago branch.

The same volumes credit a Kin-born planter, Oshiro Kozo, born in 1881, with a reputation among Japanese settlers as a benefactor of Philippine colonization and the head of a colonization company at Bago — a Davao district that still carries his name today, as Bago Oshiro, and Kin remembers him as the father of Philippine emigration, who went out with the 1904 emigration to Benguet before turning to abaca at Bago — while a Kin man named Takaesu Izo, a graduate of the prefecture's First Middle School, moved on from an early spell at Davao to head a fishery cooperative at Iloilo. Other entries follow local men into commerce in Manila and into the Japanese army: none of it as famous as the Hawaii crossing, but together the entries show that by the interwar years Kin's emigrants, and the money and letters they sent home, reached well beyond the plantations of Oahu. Some of the men named in these directories came from hamlets — Kanna, Kochiya, and the village of Ginoza itself — that were still legally part of Kin at the time, and would separate to form Ginoza village only in April 1946.

sections.heading: Invasion, occupation and a village split in two

paragraphs.text: Okinawa's prefectural archives date the war's approach to Kin precisely: reconnaissance and target photography from September 1944 through the following March, a squadron of Japanese suicide boats based at Kin and the neighboring hamlet of Yaka from January 1945, the American landing on the island's central-west coast on 1 April 1945, and the occupation of Kin village itself four days later, on 5 April. Within the year a detention camp had gone up at Yaka to hold captured Japanese soldiers along with civilians and Koreans caught up in the fighting; the site remains commemorated in the town, and Kin still holds an annual Yaka-bushi singing contest each August in honor of a folk song that local sources trace to that camp.

Remarkably, one substantial prewar building came through the battle standing: the main hall of Kin Kannon-ji, rebuilt in 1942, is described by local heritage writers as the only such wooden building on Okinawa's main island to have escaped the fires of 1945. The cave beneath it, Nisshu-do, was itself registered as a national Monument by Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs on 17 February 2026, cited for its roughly thirteen-meter-high inner chamber reached from within the temple grounds.

Occupation reorganized Kin's map as well as its economy. On 1 April 1946 the northern hamlets of the old Kin village — Kochiya (renamed Matsuda), Ginoza, Sokei and Kanna among them — were split off under the US military government to form the new village of Ginoza, whose own official history still describes the pre-1946 area as "Kin village", the same administrative unit the 1919 gazetteer and the 1930s emigrant directories describe. What remained was a smaller Kin, its old airfield on the peninsula soon repurposed: the prefectural archives record it in use as a firing range from 1947 and record fresh petitions over replacement land following a Marine Corps build-up in 1957, part of the process that made the base at Kin, later named Camp Hansen, into the fixture that still dominates the town. Camp Hansen is named for Private Dale M. Hansen, a US Marine from Nebraska awarded the Medal of Honor after his death for a one-man assault on Japanese positions on 7 May 1945; he died on Okinawa four days later. It is one of the island's installations that carry the names of eight Medal of Honor recipients of the battle.

Okinawa, including Kin, remained under US administration for twenty-seven years after the war, returning to Japanese sovereignty only in 1972; Kin itself gained formal town status, and its present name of Kin-cho, in 1980. Camp Hansen never went away in the meantime, and an exhibition drawn from the prefectural archives in 2019 put the share of Kin's total area occupied by US military facilities at roughly fifty-six percent — context for a townscape in which the base's perimeter fence is often only a street away from ordinary houses and shops.

That proximity produced its own culture. Just outside one of Camp Hansen's gates, the district known as Shinkaichi grew up from the 1950s as an entertainment strip serving the base, its bars, tailors and restaurants at their busiest during the Vietnam War years. It was here, at a small diner called Parlor Senri, that the proprietor Gibo Senri is credited by the town's own tourism authority with inventing taco rice around 1984: Mexican taco fillings spooned over plain rice instead of a tortilla, devised as a filling, inexpensive meal for young American servicemen. The dish spread across Okinawa through the 1990s and is now sold as far away as convenience stores and school lunches, but Kin still calls itself its birthplace.

Little of Kin's pre-war built fabric survived 1945, which makes the handful of true survivals worth seeking out deliberately: the 1942 hall over Nisshu's cave; and the 1935 Toyama Memorial Hall, a rare pre-war reinforced-concrete building designed by the Okinawan architect Oshiro Ryutaro and paid for, fittingly, from money left over after the town raised Toyama's statue. Used afterwards as a kindergarten, a town office and an education-board building, the hall was restored to its original appearance and reopened in October 2016, and in February 2021 it became Kin's first nationally Registered Tangible Cultural Property.

Behind the built history, the land itself still shows what the sources describe: the mangrove-lined estuary of the Okukubi River northeast of the old village center, cited today as the only place on Okinawa's main island where all four native mangrove species grow together, sits exactly where the 1919 gazetteer placed Kin's spring-fed lowland, and the wells and taro paddies still worked in the valley draw on the same limestone groundwater the old sources took for granted. Aerial coverage available for this dossier's companion photo pages begins only in the 1970s, after reversion; the US forces who administered Okinawa before then held their own imagery of the landing beaches and the airfield years earlier; readers wanting to see Kin during the occupation itself will need to look to American, not Japanese, archives.

timeline.what: The monk Nisshu is said to wash ashore at Kin's port of Fukka and found Kin Kannon-ji over a limestone cave.
Kin exists as an established Ryukyuan magiri (district), its bounds reaching inland to hamlets that will not separate until 1946.
Land is cut from Nago and Kin to found the new district of Kushi, in the kingdom's own administrative reorganization.
Toyama Kyuzo organizes Okinawa's first group emigration; the party reaches Honolulu on 8 January 1900, twenty-six strong, ten of them from Kin.
Toyama writes that about 5,000 Okinawans have emigrated under his arrangements, chiefly to Hawaii.
Japan's Hydrographic Department surveys Kin Bay and Cape, romanizing the name as "Chimu".
Kin villagers land at Davao in the Philippines to grow abaca on plantations run by firms such as Ota Kogyo.
The Toyama Memorial Hall is completed in Kin, designed by Oshiro Ryutaro.
Wartime conditions end overseas emigration; the town's own count puts Kin's total emigrants sent since 1899 at about 3,225.
US forces land on Okinawa's central-west coast and occupy Kin village within days; a detention camp is soon set up at Yaka.
Kochiya, Ginoza, Sokei and Kanna separate from Kin village to form Ginoza village under the US military government.
The former Kin airfield becomes a US forces firing range, then, after a 1957 Marine build-up, the base later named Camp Hansen.
Okinawa reverts to Japanese sovereignty in 1972; Kin gains town status in 1980.
Gibo Senri is credited with inventing taco rice at Parlor Senri in Kin's Shinkaichi entertainment district.
The Toyama Memorial Hall reopens after restoration (2016) and is registered as a cultural property (2021); Kin Kannon-ji's cave is registered as a national Monument (17 February 2026).

walk.name: Kin Kannon-ji and Nisshu-do cave
walk.ja: 金峯山金武観音寺・日秀洞
walk.what: A 1942 wooden hall, said to be the only one of its kind on Okinawa's main island to have escaped the 1945 battle, stands over a limestone cave whose roughly 13-meter inner chamber was registered a national Monument in February 2026; look for the shrine-and-temple images sharing the same precinct, a survival of pre-Meiji religious practice.

walk.name: Toyama Memorial Hall
walk.what: A 1935 reinforced-concrete hall with a curved, beamless ceiling and round windows, designed by Oshiro Ryutaro and funded from the surplus of Toyama Kyuzo's statue fund; restored and reopened in 2016 and registered as a national cultural property in 2021, it now displays material on Kin's emigration history; admission is free, weekdays 9:00-16:00.

walk.name: Toyama Kyuzo's statue and the "World Stone"
walk.ja: 當山久三の像・世界石
walk.what: A statue of the emigration pioneer stands near the memorial hall; a verse stone nearby, which villagers came to call the "World Stone", carries Toyama's own call to leave for the wider world, a companion to a matching stone later placed at the Hawaii Okinawa Center.

walk.name: Yaka
walk.what: The hamlet north of the old village center where a US detention camp held Japanese soldiers, civilians and Koreans from 1945; the town's annual Yaka-bushi singing contest each August commemorates a folk song local histories trace to the camp.

walk.name: Shinkaichi and the taco rice diners
walk.what: The strip of bars and restaurants that grew up outside a Camp Hansen gate from the 1950s; a diner here is credited with inventing taco rice around 1984 to feed young servicemen cheaply and quickly.
walk.photoNone: No Commons photo of the Shinkaichi strip or its taco rice diners

walk.name: Okukubi River mangroves
walk.what: An estuary northeast of the town center where all four mangrove species found on the Okinawan mainland grow; the spring-fed valley behind it still carries the taro paddies and wells that the area's limestone groundwater has supported for generations.

deepResearchLeads.what: Labor contracts and company records for Okinawan abaca workers at Davao
deepResearchLeads.where: 外交史料館 (Diplomatic Archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs), Tokyo, which holds pre-war passport and emigration-company records; Philippine-side archives in Davao/Manila
deepResearchLeads.how: Request pre-war passport registers (旅券下付表) for Kunigami County by name; for the Philippine side, consult the Ateneo de Davao University's research collections on the pre-war Japanese community.

caveats: The 1919 Kunigami County gazetteer (S1) that this dossier leans on for early geography and history — the peaks and prewar ports, and the date of Kushi district's separation from Kin and Nago (1674 in the original research's reading of the gazetteer) — could not be retrieved as searchable text in this fact-check session (the online full-text index refused this book), so those specific details rest on the original research rather than an independent re-check here; a widely repeated secondary account instead dates the Kushi separation to 1673.

Details of the wartime detention camp at Yaka (numbers held, exact closure date) are reported in secondary sources this dossier could not verify directly; only what the Prefectural Archives' own exhibition and a library reference answer support is stated here.

The share of Kin's land occupied by US military facilities is given as an official exhibition reported it in 2019 (about 56 percent); current, precise figures were not independently retrieved in this session.
